title: MS-Eval: Benchmarking Sub-Agent Delegation and Orchestration in MCP-Intensive Working Scenarios

Title:MS-Eval: Benchmarking Sub-Agent Delegation and Orchestration in MCP-Intensive Working Scenarios
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:LLM agents are increasingly integrated into real-world works, yet they must handle diverse domain-specific tools and complex multi-sub-task problems that sequential tool invocation resolves inefficiently and with severe context bloat. The Main-Agent Delegation and Sub-Agent Execution (MAD-SAE) paradigm addresses these issues by delegating sub-tasks to specialized sub-agents for parallel execution in isolated contexts, but its delegation and orchestration quality remains unquantified. We introduce MS-Eval, a unified evaluation kit comprising an MCP-intensive benchmark, a controlled execution harness, tailored delegation and orchestration metrics, and the MSQ index for comprehensive assessment. Evaluating four MAD-SAE variants and eight frontier models reveals that (1) sub-agent specialization (Spec) is the best practical practice; (2) open-source models are largely competitive with few exceptions; and (3) MAD-SAE generally raises cost with contingent payoff, benefiting most open-source models in both performance and efficiency while leaving closed-source models with higher cost and degraded performance. Our case study further traces these gains to better single-agent solutions, effective context offloading, and genuine sub-task parallelism, whereas unnecessary or redundant delegation turns the same cost into pure overhead. report.summary: MS-Eval introduces a benchmark and metrics to quantify how LLM main agents delegate sub-tasks to specialized sub-agents in MCP-heavy workflows.
report.background: LLM agents increasingly rely on domain-specific tools, often exposed through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), to complete real-world work. Sequential tool calls become inefficient and cause context bloat when tasks are complex and span multiple sub-tasks. The Main-Agent Delegation and Sub-Agent Execution (MAD-SAE) paradigm addresses this by splitting work among specialized sub-agents that run in isolated contexts, potentially in parallel. But until now, the quality of delegation and orchestration in this pattern was not systematically measured. MS-Eval fills that gap with an MCP-intensive benchmark, a controlled execution harness, tailored metrics, and the MSQ index. It evaluates four MAD-SAE variants and eight frontier models, offering the first structured evidence on when sub-agent delegation helps, when it adds overhead, and how model choice affects outcomes.
key_points: MS-Eval is a unified evaluation kit for agent delegation: it combines an MCP-intensive benchmark, a controlled execution harness, delegation and orchestration metrics, and the MSQ index for overall scoring. This gives researchers a repeatable way to compare orchestration strategies rather than relying on anecdotal demos.

Sub-agent specialization is the strongest practical pattern. Across four MAD-SAE variants, the specialized-sub-agent setup performed best, suggesting that assigning narrow roles and tools to sub-agents beats generic delegation for complex MCP-heavy tasks.

Open-source models are largely competitive with closed-source models in these orchestration tests, with only a few exceptions. This challenges assumptions that frontier closed models automatically dominate when agents must delegate and coordinate tool use.

MAD-SAE raises cost with conditional payoff. It helped most open-source models in both performance and efficiency, but closed-source models often paid higher cost with degraded performance, meaning delegation is not universally beneficial.

Case studies trace gains to better single-agent solutions, effective context offloading, and genuine sub-task parallelism. Unnecessary or redundant delegation turns the same coordination cost into pure overhead, so orchestration quality matters as much as model quality.
report.impact: MS-Eval gives the AI industry a shared yardstick for agent orchestration, an area that has grown quickly but lacked rigorous measurement. For developers, the lesson is to design specialized sub-agents, isolate context deliberately, and parallelize only genuinely independent work; blind delegation can increase latency and cost without improving results. Model choice also matters: open-source models may deliver better orchestration economics, while closed-source models may need more careful prompting or simpler single-agent designs. For regular users, better orchestration should mean more reliable multi-step assistants that handle tool-heavy tasks without losing context. But the benchmark also warns that agentic complexity can silently raise operating costs, so product teams should validate delegation against simpler baselines before shipping.
report.tools: Watch the MS-Eval code release and benchmark harness for reproducible testing. For hands-on work, explore MCP reference servers and SDKs, plus orchestration frameworks such as LangGraph, AutoGen, CrewAI, OpenAI Agents SDK, and Claude Agent SDK. These let developers compare single-agent, specialized sub-agent, and parallel delegation patterns before adopting them in production.
